result.summary: The poet invokes the Muses and sets out his theme, the war of Oedipus' sons for Thebes. Oedipus prays to the Fury Tisiphone, Jove plans war with Juno protesting, and Polynices and Tydeus fight at Adrastus' door in Argos. Adrastus recognizes them as his destined sons-in-law and tells the story of Apollo, Coroebus and the monster.

scenes.title: Invocation and theme
scenes.summary: The poet asks the Muses where to begin, declines to start with Cadmus, and turns aside to praise the emperor before settling on the war of the brothers.

scenes.title: Oedipus prays for vengeance
scenes.summary: The blind Oedipus calls on Tisiphone to set his sons against each other, and she hears him.
scenes.stakes: Oedipus risks nothing; his sons are doomed by his curse.

scenes.title: The Fury sows discord
scenes.summary: Tisiphone rises from the underworld to Thebes and inspires the brothers with hatred. They agree to alternate rule, and Eteocles keeps the throne while Polynices is exiled.
scenes.stakes: The brothers risk their lives and city for sole power.

scenes.title: A Theban grumbles
scenes.summary: A citizen complains of the unstable alternating rule and the omen of Cadmus' sown warriors.
scenes.stakes: The people suffer from uncertain rulers.

scenes.title: Council of the gods
scenes.summary: Jove resolves to punish the houses of Thebes and Argos. Juno pleads for Argos, but Jove swears by the Styx and sends Mercury to the underworld to fetch Laius' shade.
scenes.stakes: Argos and Thebes face destruction; Juno fears for her favoured city.

scenes.title: Polynices' storm-tossed journey
scenes.summary: Polynices travels by night through a great storm to Argos and falls asleep at Adrastus' door.
scenes.stakes: Polynices faces storm and wild beasts on his journey.

scenes.title: Fight at Adrastus' gate
scenes.summary: Tydeus arrives and fights Polynices. King Adrastus stops them, and sees an omen of his oracle.
scenes.stakes: Both youths risk killing each other.

scenes.title: Feast in Adrastus' hall
scenes.summary: Adrastus sees the lion and boar skins, recognizes the oracle, and holds a feast, with his daughters appearing.

scenes.title: Tale of Coroebus
scenes.summary: Adrastus tells how Apollo's child by Crotopus' daughter died, a monster killed Argive infants, and Coroebus slew it and offered himself to Apollo.
scenes.stakes: Coroebus offers his life to end Apollo's plague on Argos.

scenes.title: Names revealed and hymn
scenes.summary: Polynices admits he is a Theban, and Adrastus consoles him and leads a hymn to Phoebus.
scenes.stakes: Polynices is ashamed of his cursed lineage.

Opening statement of the poem's theme of fratricidal strife.

analysis.text: The book shows inherited guilt: Oedipus' curse, the Fury and Jove's wrath drive the brothers toward ruin, and power-hunger overrides kinship.
Statius' proem flatters the Flavian emperor Domitian, reflecting the poet's court setting under Roman imperial rule.

legacy.text: Statius' Thebaid was widely read in the Middle Ages and influenced Dante, who makes Statius a character in the Purgatorio, and Chaucer.

fun_facts.text: Statius spent about twelve years writing the Thebaid, finishing it around 92 CE.

language_notes.text: Pierian: of Pieria, home of the Muses; 'Pierian fire' means poetic inspiration. 'Alternate reign' is the brothers' agreed yearly rule of Thebes.
The Sidonian rape is Jove's abduction of Europa; her brother Cadmus, sent by their father Agenor to find her, went on to found Thebes.
The husbandman sowing battles is Cadmus, who sowed dragon's teeth from which armed men sprang. Amphion's song moved stones to build Thebes' walls.
Athamas, driven mad by Juno, hunted his son; his wife Ino leapt into the sea holding Palaemon, becoming a sea goddess.
The standards, Rhine, Ister (Danube) and Dacians refer to the emperor Domitian's northern campaigns, which the poet postpones as a theme.
Aonian means Boeotian, the region of Thebes. 'Lernaean gore' is the blood of Argives, from Lerna near Argos.
The laurel-crowned prophet is Amphiaraus, swallowed alive by a chasm in the earth during the war.
Oedipus recounts his story: exposed as an infant with pierced feet, he killed Laius at the crossroads, solved the Sphinx's riddle, and married his mother Jocasta.
Cirrha is the port near Delphi, where Oedipus sought the oracle. Polybus was the Corinthian king who raised him.
Taenarus, in southern Laconia, was believed to hold a cave entrance to the underworld, so the Fury is leaving Hades by it.
"Hies her" means hurries; "hies" is archaic, and "her" is reflexive.
Thessalian ("Atracian") witches were said to draw down the moon by spells, making it look red and troubled in an eclipse. Phoebe is the moon.
Atropos is the Fate who cuts the thread of life; Proserpine is queen of the dead. Both are linked with death.
"Cadmean towers" means Thebes, founded by Cadmus. "Wonted gloom" is the habitual darkness this cursed house has always had.
"Coulter" is the iron blade fixed before a plough's share; "fain" means gladly or eagerly.
Dirce is a spring and stream near Thebes; "Tyrian exile" is Cadmus, who came from Tyre in Phoenicia.
Oedipus, father of the brothers, ruled Thebes before them; his cursed legacy underlies their quarrel.
"Echionian" means Theban, from Echion, one of the Spartoi, the men sprung from the dragon's teeth, ancestors of the Thebans.
Ogygian: Theban. Ogyges was a legendary early king associated with Thebes, so the poet uses the word as a poetic synonym for Theban.
Cadmus searched for his sister Europa, carried off by Jove as a bull. Told to found a city, he sowed dragon's teeth and armed men sprang up and fought each other.
The Cyclopes forged Jove's thunderbolts in Vulcan's smithies; 'Aeolian' refers to the volcanic Aeolian islands, where the forges were placed.
Phaethon borrowed the Sun's chariot, lost control and was struck down by Jove's lightning, nearly burning the world.
Oedipus unknowingly killed his father Laius and married his mother Jocasta.
Jove killed Argus, guardian of Io (the Pharian heifer), and came to Danae in a shower of gold. Both are Argive stories of his infidelity.
Oenomaus killed suitors of his daughter Hippodamia in chariot races until Pelops defeated him; the site lay at Olympia, by the Alpheus.
The gods' most binding oath was by the river Styx; it could not be broken.
Cyllenian: Mercury, named from Mount Cyllene, his birthplace. Laius is to be summoned from the underworld.
Aonia is a poetic name for Boeotia, the region around Thebes, so he is still crossing his homeland.
Inachian and Danaan both mean Argive; Inachus was Argos' river-god and Danaus a legendary Argive king. Mycenae stands for Argolis generally.
Mycenae is 'dark with the sun's withdrawal' because of the Thyestean banquet, when the sun turned back from Atreus' horrid feast.
Ogygian means Theban (from the old king Ogyges). The 'Bacchic gore' recalls the Theban women who tore Pentheus apart in Bacchic frenzy.
Sciron was a robber who kicked travellers off cliffs; Scylla's country is Megara, where Scylla betrayed her father Nisus, the purple-haired king.
The 'Titanian queen' is the Moon, called so as a descendant of the Titans; her 'dewy chariot' is the moon's car.
Aeolia is the home of the winds, imprisoned in caves by Aeolus. Auster is the south wind and Boreas the north.
The 'Wain' is the Great Bear constellation, used by sailors for navigation; 'Cadmean' means Theban, after Cadmus, founder of Thebes.
Lerna's marsh was where Hercules killed the Hydra, burning its necks with fire, hence 'branded by Herculean fire'.
Apollo's oracle said his daughters' husbands would come as a boar and a lion; this is fulfilled when Tydeus (boar emblem) and Polynices (lion) arrive.
Amphiaraus is the Argive seer, yet even he cannot interpret the prophecy because Apollo, his patron god, forbids him.
Olenian means from Olenus, a place in Aetolia; here it simply marks Tydeus as Aetolian, from Calydon.
Tydeus fled Calydon after killing a kinsman (the text says a brother); the 'former stranger' is Polynices, who sheltered at the porch earlier.
Rhipaean refers to the Rhipaean mountains, a legendary northern range associated with harsh storms and hail.
The Pisaean Thunderer is Jove at Olympia in Pisa; his festival every fifth year is the Olympic Games.
Achaean here means Greek, specifically Argive.
Tydeus cites Centaurs and Cyclopes, savage beings who still live at peace with their own kind, to shame Polynices for refusing to share shelter.
Theseus and Pirithous, and Orestes and Pylades, were legendary pairs of devoted friends.
Amphitryon's son is Hercules, who killed the Nemean lion; here the poet places the kill in the Teumesian glades, and the skin became his garment.
The spoils of Calydon are the hide of the Calydonian boar, which Tydeus wears; its bristles and tusk echo the oracle's beasts.
Apollo's oracle told Adrastus his daughters would marry a lion and a boar; the strangers' pelts now seem to fulfil this riddle.
Lustral entrails are the inner organs of sacrificed victims, offered in purification rites and burned on the altar.
The mystic Tripod and grotto mean Apollo's oracle at Delphi, where the priestess prophesied seated on a tripod.
Bloodless flesh means meat drained of blood, or cooked until no blood showed, ready to eat.
Son of Iasus means Adrastus, descended from Iasus of Argos; Danaus and Phoroneus were legendary earlier kings of Argos.
The winged youth is Perseus, who beheaded the Gorgon Medusa; the goblet's engraving shows him in flight with her head.
The Phrygian hunter is Ganymede, carried off by Jove's eagle to be cupbearer of the gods; Gargara is a peak of Mount Ida near Troy.
Apollo's slaying of the serpent Python at Delphi; Cirrha was Delphi's port-town. The killing required purification, so he sought expiation at Crotopus' house.
"The Delian" is Apollo, named from his birthplace Delos.
Cynthia is the moon; twice five times full means ten lunar months of pregnancy.
The monster is Poine, the avenging spirit sent by Apollo; Acheron is a river of the underworld.
"Nether Jove" means Pluto, lord of the underworld, to whom the monster is returned.
"Inachian" means Argive, from Inachus, the river and founder-king of Argos.
Paean is a title of Apollo as healer; Sirius, the dog star, signified scorching heat and plague.
Thymbraean is an epithet of Apollo, from his shrine at Thymbra near Troy.
Adrastus has overheard the youths' earlier quarrel and infers Tydeus is son of Oeneus of Calydon.
"Ismenian" means Theban, from the river Ismenus near Thebes.
Refers to Oedipus' reign, his incest, and his self-blinding in shame, known throughout the world.
Apollo and Poseidon built Troy's walls for Laomedon, who cheated them of payment; hence "thankless shoulders."

context_notes.text: The Muses are invoked for guidance, as in epic tradition.
Clio is the Muse of history, here called on to choose the first hero.
Tisiphone is one of the three Furies, avenging spirits who punish crimes, especially against kin.
Cocytus is a river of the underworld, whose name means lamentation.
Tisiphone is one of the three Furies, spirits of vengeance, sent here to drive the sons of Oedipus to hatred.
Atlas is the Titan who holds up the sky on his shoulders, here shaken by the Fury's passing.
Palaemon was a child god of the sea; his mother Ino leapt into the sea with him, and here she saves him from the Fury's noise.
The brothers are Eteocles and Polynices, sons of Oedipus, who agree to rule Thebes in alternate years.
Jove (the Greek Zeus) is king of the gods; the council meets in the heavens, to decide Thebes' and Argos' fate.
Tantalus served his son Pelops to the gods at a banquet. He was the ancestor of the Argive royal house.
Juno complains that Egyptian cults of Isis, at Coptos and the Nile, receive more joyful worship than she does.
Mercury, grandson of Atlas, is the gods' messenger. He wears winged sandals and a broad hat (petasus).
Polynices, exiled son of Oedipus, was supposed to share the Theban throne with his brother Eteocles in alternate years, but Eteocles refused to yield it.
The 'kinsman' is his brother Eteocles, who held the throne after the agreed year and drove Polynices out.
Polynices is heading for Argos, ruled by King Adrastus, where he will find refuge and an ally against Thebes.
Nemea, Arcadia, Inachus and Erasinus are places and rivers of the Peloponnese, so the storm sweeps the whole Argive region he enters.
Larissa was the citadel of Argos, whose appearance signals the end of his journey.
Adrastus is king of Argos. His line goes back to Jove through both parents' ancestry, as the text says.
Oeneus was king of Calydon and Tydeus' father. Mars, god of war, is claimed as an ancestor.
Polynices hesitates because he is the exiled son of Oedipus, whose name carries a curse and shame.
Phoebus is Apollo, god of prophecy. Adrastus had been warned by his oracle to marry his daughters to a lion and a boar.
Acaste is the nurse who guards the king's daughters, Argia and Deipyle, until they are married.
Diana is the virgin huntress goddess and Pallas is Minerva, goddess of war; both are chaste, so they suit the maidens.
Apollo killed Python at Delphi; Castalia was the sacred spring there.
The Sisters are the Fates, who spin and cut the thread of each life.
Polynices reveals he is son of Oedipus and Jocasta, from the cursed house of Cadmus, Thebes' founder.
The hymn lists Apollo's punishments: Tityos for assaulting Latona, Phlegyas for burning Delphi's temple, and Marsyas the Phrygian.

literary_notes.text: The poet announces the epic theme and claims divine inspiration, following the convention of Homer and Virgil.
The poet addresses the emperor directly, urging him to stay on earth rather than become a god, a flattering conceit.
The 'fierce daylight of the mind' with 'unwearied wings' makes guilty memory a bird tormenting the blind man.
Oedipus lists his past deeds as if they earned the Fury's favour, though they were disasters he suffered.
'Cruel, pitiful punishment' joins opposites to show his blindness as both severe and deserving of pity.
The Fury letting her snakes drink from sulphurous waters gives a vivid, casual picture of horror.
Snakes, iron-coloured eyes and venomous breath create a vivid, grotesque portrait of the Fury as a figure of plague and death.
Passions such as envy, fear and ambition are listed as forces entering the brothers' hearts, making their ruin seem inevitable.
The brothers are compared to two wild bullocks yoked together, each pulling against the other and wrecking the furrows.
The narrator directly addresses the brothers with rhetorical questions, lamenting that their quarrel is over so small a prize.
The praise of Eteocles' proud day is undercut by what follows, as murmurs of discontent already begin.
The citizens are compared to sails buffeted by opposing winds, showing helplessness under rival rulers.
Jove's calm, silent authority makes the gods tremble and wait for his permission to sit, establishing his majesty.
Jove sarcastically says Oedipus's prayers are answered, turning the blind man's curse on his sons into the instrument of divine vengeance.
Juno, goddess of marriage, resentfully pardons Jove's hidden affairs while hating the cities that expose his infidelity.
The air is made to receive Mercury, and he shudders at its frailness, giving vivid physical sense to the descent.
The year is imagined standing still in its slow constellations, showing Polynices' impatience through how he perceives time.
Sleep steals, stoops and beckons like a kindly person, softening the night just before the storm's violence.
The winds struggle for mastery of the sky like rival armies, foreshadowing the brothers' coming war.
The raging storm mirrors Polynices' fear and turmoil, as the thought of his brother assails him.
Polynices is compared to a lost sailor in a storm, making his stumbling through the dark forest a sea-voyage of peril.
The oracle of a boar and a lion prepares for the arrival of the two brawling strangers.
Tydeus is shown as smaller but more valiant, establishing his fierce spirit in contrast to the taller Theban.
The fight is compared to Olympic athletes, but the poet stresses the difference: these men fight from hate, not for glory.
The narrator addresses Polynices directly, saying death would have been 'far better', a hint of the doom awaiting him and his brother.
Anger fading is compared to a storm-tossed sea calming while a last breath still stirs the sails, showing lingering resentment.
Polynices' lion skin is compared to Hercules' first trophy, casting the exile as a heroic figure with a mighty destiny.
Frozen silence set against the thrill of joy shows Adrastus' outward shock and inward delight at the oracle's fulfilment.
Adrastus addresses Night directly as a goddess, thanking her for revealing the oracle's meaning.
The daughters are likened to Diana and Pallas, but lacking their terror, which stresses their gentle beauty.
The description of the goblet's art makes the gold seem alive, as Medusa almost moves and pales.
The narrator addresses the dead infant directly, heightening pathos as the humble cradle contrasts with his divine birth.
The interjection "Oh horrible!" shows Adrastus' own horror at Crotopus' cruelty.
"They can—yet cannot glut their ire" captures rage that no mutilation can satisfy.
Apollo is shown as a vengeful archer on Parnassus, making plague his arrows.
Coroebus calls Apollo "ruthless" and "most righteous" together, mocking the god's unjust demand.
Repeating "my life" stresses Coroebus' self-sacrificing resolve.
